items.titel: Supermarket cyberattacks in Europe hit Italy's Coop stores in Catania and Palermo
items.anriss: On Monday night a cyberattack hit dozens of supermarkets in six European countries, raising fridge temperatures to 50°C and spoiling tonnes of food. Four Coop stores in Sicily were also damaged.

absaetze.t: Published on 4 November 2026 - 9:43 GMT+1

The hacker attack that hit around a hundred supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Estonia and Ireland has not spared Italy. At least four Coop stores, three in Catania and one in Palermo, were affected by a suspected cyberattack that caused temperatures to rise in refrigeration systems and forced shopkeepers to throw away food that had overheated.
ADVERTISEMENT

This was initially reported to Ansa by Giuseppe Spadaro, general manager of the Radenza group, which runs the Coop supermarkets. "We have verified that it is an attack on our remote control system for frozen-food counters. After a careful screening it appears there is no further damage, but the attack did take place," later confirmed Coop Radenza's chief executive, Danilo Radenza.
Reports of incidents also at companies in Tuscany and Emilia Romagna

According to Spadaro, the postal police are reconstructing the origin and scale of the attacks and checking whether there are links with what has happened in other European countries. "We are calculating the damage. In some cases we have fixed the problem.We have already contacted the National Cybersecurity Agency and activated protocols to carry out in depth investigations," said the Radenza director.

The National Cybersecurity Agency (Acn) said it has received reports of an incident affecting a Tuscan company in the collective catering sector and has detected an attack against a company in Emilia that produces frozen foods.

Acn has recommended urgently checking whether control and remote assistance systems used by food distribution chains are exposed on the Internet, as well as strengthening remote access via VPNs and multi factor authentication, reviewing privileged accounts and updating or replacing devices that are no longer supported by manufacturers, Ansa reports.
A meeting is scheduled for tomorrow between the Agency, sector federations and the main national large scale retail companies.
The previous hacker attack on supermarkets in France on 12 October

The postal police are investigating possible links with the incidents that occurred in other European countries. The Parliamentary Committee for the Security of the Republic (Copasir) will also request information from the government on Tuesday.

The cyberattack took place at around four in the morning and pushed refrigerator temperatures in the affected supermarkets in Europe above 50 degrees, with retailers finding themselves at opening time forced to throw away spoiled food.

The European Union has described the situation as "highly worrying". On 12 October, another cyberattack had already hit the main supermarket chains in France, causing losses of millions of euros. No one has yet claimed responsibility for the attacks but there appear to be few doubts that the incidents are connected.

To investigate what has happened, Palazzo Chigi has decided to convene a meeting to be attended by the Director of the National Cybersecurity Agency and the heads of the intelligence agencies, coordinated by the undersecretary to the prime minister's office Alfredo Mantovano.

items.titel: Finnish president phones Middle East leaders about Ukraine
items.anriss: Alexander Stubb held phone calls with the leaders of Egypt, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday.

absaetze.t: Alexander Stubb held phone calls with the leaders of Egypt, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has spoken by phone to the heads of three Middle Eastern countries, he said in a post on X.
He spoke to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Qatari PM Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
Stubb said they discussed the situation in the Middle East and Russia's war in Ukraine, among other topics.
"The common denominator in all these calls was the recognition of the need to promote peace and stability in both regions, and the readiness to work towards these goals," he said on X.

Stubb's call follows a joint phone call he made with the Norwegian prime minister to Russian President Vladimir Putin last week. According to Stubb's office, the aim was to give Putin a direct message ahead of the upcoming negotiations in Abu Dhabi, which are intended to help end Russia's war in Ukraine.

items.titel: EU cancer groups fear funding squeeze under next long-term budget
items.anriss: As European Union countries negotiate funding allocations for the bloc’s next long-term budget, cancer organisations fear that projects spanning from research to personalised care and patient support could be discontinued, weakening cancer …

absaetze.t: The European Union's next long-term budget, covering the 2028–2034 period, will determine how the bloc allocates funding across its policy priorities, including health.
ADVERTISEMENT

Under the European Commission’s proposal, health funding would share a common pot with biotechnology, agriculture and the bioeconomy, all placed under a broader European Competitiveness Fund. EU countries have adopted a partial negotiating position on the proposed fund, although its final structure and specific funding allocations remain subject to negotiations.

Cancer organisations fear that not having a dedicated pot for health risks losing financial backing for already ongoing cancer projects, which span from cancer prevention and vaccination to research into new diagnostics and patient support.

Moreover, projects are funded as part of the EU's Beating Cancer Plan and Cancer Mission — Europe's cancer-fighting initiatives backed by a standalone health budget and the EU’s research fund Horizon Europe — both set to run until 2030, overlapping with the first years of the next long-term budget, which will run from 2028 until 2034.
As the agreement on the next long-term budget between the countries is expected by the end of the year, organizations are using one of their last windows of opportunity to lobby for more.

“Projects that are making a real difference – training doctors, giving young people with cancer a voice and developing treatments where options are limited – now face an uncertain future,” Isabel Rubio, president of the European Cancer Organisation, told Euronews.
One project bracing itself for uncertainty is ECHoS, which works to support the implementation of EU cancer actions at the national and regional levels.
“We navigate the uncertainty, always hoping for the best but in a way preparing for the worst,” Hugo Soares, ECHoS co-coordinator, told Euronews.
Soares said it would be a lost opportunity to stop investing in projects with promising technology, therapies or developments.

“We don't expect it to be sustained by the Commission forever, because it's not doable and you have other priorities, but this is something that you should have a phase-out strategy, rather than getting to 2030 and cutting everything,” he said.

However, a Commission spokesperson told Euronews that under the Commission’s proposal, measures currently financed through EU4Health — EU’s standalone health budget — would “generally be eligible” to seek competitive funding under the next long-term budget, “offering a route to support relevant health actions in the next funding period and ensuring a smooth transition”.

National and Regional Partnership Plans would support national healthcare systems, the Competitiveness Fund would aim to foster innovation and competitiveness in the health sector, and Horizon Europe would continue to fund research, the spokesperson said.
That is also backed by countries — which have the final say on the next budget.

Germany’s Federal Ministry of Health told Euronews that all projects previously eligible for EU4Health funding should remain eligible under the new budget, adding that the new structure allows strengthening the “Health in all policies” approach at EU level.

Currently, the Commission’s proposed Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for the next seven years is in countries’ hands. In June 2026, they agreed to keep the Commission's proposed structure. Negotiations are aimed at reaching an agreement by the end of the year, the Council told Euronews.
Countries have already reached a provisional agreement
Not all countries that Euronews spoke to are sharing Germany’s optimism.
Some countries, such as Spain, have unsuccessfully pushed for a standalone health programme under the new long-term budget.

Spain has defended operating grants for civil society health organisations and argued that health “should have a role separated from a Competitiveness Fund,” Javier Sanchez Padilla, the country's Secretary of Health, told Euronews. However, he acknowledged that the trend is “putting everything in the competitiveness basket.”

Luxembourg’s Health Ministry told Euronews it is worried about the visibility and continuity of EU public health funding, particularly for prevention, health promotion and the exchange of best practices between health authorities, while Slovenia has asked for safeguards to guarantee health investment.
Estonia argued that the key safeguards will lie in the fund’s multiannual work programmes, which will determine allocations, supported activities and co-financing rules.
What does the Parliament say?
Members of the European Parliament have also raised concerns about the proposed structure.

Vytenis Andriukaitis, a member of the Socialists & Democrats group, told Euronews that the Competitiveness Fund was more focused on industry and that prevention programmes risked receiving less attention.

“The Competitiveness Fund is targeted more at industry. It is for the health industry too, but prevention programmes will be far from the attention, and it is clear that we will have huge challenges because of that,” he said.

Parliament’s public health committee has called for EU4Health to remain a standalone programme and for Horizon Europe to receive more funding for healthcare prevention. In a report adopted on 28 September, it called for at least €10.05 billion for health in the 2028–2034 EU budget, including €2.5 billion specifically earmarked for cancer action.
Parliament cannot amend the long-term budget text but holds a veto: the Council can only adopt the regulation once Parliament has given its consent by an absolute majority.

The European Cancer Organisation is making a similar call. It says the next EU long-term budget must allocate at least €10 billion for health, including at least €2 billion for a dedicated cancer fund. It also wants the money protected from competition with industrial and commercial priorities, and long-term funding commitments.
“It makes no sense for Europe to invest millions in programmes that save lives, only to let them disappear because we’ve allowed the funding to dry up,” Rubio added.

items.titel: BMW erwirtschaftet noch weniger Gewinn
items.anriss: Die Absatzkrise in China lässt den Gewinn von BMW im dritten Quartal weiter einbrechen. Auch teure Abfindungen und das vorgezogene Aus älterer Modelle verhageln dem Münchner Autobauer die Bilanz.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Die Absatzkrise in China lässt den Gewinn von BMW im dritten Quartal weiter einbrechen. Auch teure Abfindungen und das vorgezogene Aus älterer Modelle verhageln dem Münchner Autobauer die Bilanz.

BMW macht immer weniger Gewinn. Im dritten Quartal hat der Konzern nach Steuern 1,45 Milliarden Euro verdient, wie der Autohersteller mitteilte. Das waren knapp 15 Prozent weniger als vor einem Jahr. Zudem sind die Aussichten für das laufende vierte Quartal nach einer Gewinnwarnung am Dienstagabend schlecht.

Entscheidender Treiber für den Rückgang ist die Krise im China-Geschäft. Wie alle deutschen Hersteller leidet BMW darunter, dass der wichtigste Automarkt der Welt schrumpft und gleichzeitig von immer stärkerer Konkurrenz und heftigen Preiskämpfen geschüttelt wird. Auch BMW büßte dort rund ein Viertel seines Absatzes ein.

Die Münchner sind allerdings nicht so stark vom chinesischen Markt abhängig wie beispielsweise die VW-Tochter Audi. Zudem hatte der Konzern zumindest einen Teil der Rückgänge durch Zuwächse in Europa und den USA auffangen können, sodass der Absatz nur um 6,3 Prozent nachgab. Der Umsatz sank minimal langsamer um 5,8 Prozent auf 30,5 Milliarden Euro.
Schon die zweite Gewinnwarnung

Schon am Vorabend der Quartalszahlen hatte BMW eine Gewinnwarnung herausgegeben. Es war bereits die zweite innerhalb von nur fünf Monaten. Die Gewinn-Marge im Autogeschäft wird für das laufende Jahr nun zwischen minus 0,5 und plus 0,5 Prozent erwartet. Bisher lag die Prognose bei 1 bis 3 Prozent. Das bedeutet, dass das Unternehmen im Kerngeschäft Geld verlieren könnte. Schuld ist ausgerechnet der Erfolg des Sparprogramms, dessen Kosten - zusammen mit anderen Effekten - auf die Profitabilität drücken.

Das im Sommer angekündigte Programm war Anfang Oktober gestartet und nach nicht einmal drei Wochen bereits wieder geschlossen worden, weil das Interesse der Mitarbeiter, gegen eine oft deutlich sechsstellige Zahlungen das Unternehmen zu verlassen, überraschend groß war. Aus früheren Aussagen geht hervor, dass BMW mit gut einer Milliarde Euro an Kosten rechnete. Weitere Kosten entstehen dadurch, dass die Münchner ältere Modelle früher als ursprünglich geplant auslaufen lassen.

BMW-Finanzchef Walter Mertl bezeichnete die Belastungen als Investition in die Zukunft. "Geschwindigkeit ist bei unserer geplanten Neuausrichtung ein Erfolgsfaktor. Deshalb intensivieren wir noch in diesem Jahr die Maßnahmen für mehr Effizienz und schlankere Strukturen", sagte er. "Damit wollen wir unsere künftigen Margen stärken." Auch Konzernchef Milan Nedeljkovic betonte die Bedeutung des Tempos: "Die Entwicklung in unserer Industrie erfordert konsequente Entscheidungen und schnelle Umsetzung. Wir werden daher strukturelle Maßnahmen gezielt intensivieren und beschleunigen."
Schwieriges Schlussquartal

Auch die Erwartungen für den Absatz hat BMW gesenkt. Der Konzern geht jetzt von einem moderaten Rückgang aus - das entspricht 5 bis 9,9 Prozent. Bisher hatte der Ausblick hier von einem leichten Rückgang um 1 bis 4,9 Prozent gesprochen. Die Prognose für den Gewinn vor Steuern ließ BMW unangetastet. Hier geht der Konzern allerdings bereits seit der ersten Gewinnwarnung im Frühsommer von einem deutlichen Rückgang aus. Das wären mehr als 15 Prozent.
Mit seinem Ergebnis im dritten Quartal schneidet BMW minimal schlechter ab als Konkurrent Mercedes, der auf 1,52 Milliarden Euro Gewinn kam, allerdings sehr viel besser als Audi und VW.
BMW-Aktie verliert
Papiere von BMW hatten schon am Dienstagabend im nachbörslichen Handel verloren. Am Mittwochmorgen tendierten sie zum Handelsbeginn uneinheitlich.

items.titel: The G.I. and the Paperback: A World War II Love Story
items.anriss: On June 5, 1944, as soldiers lined British shores, preparing for their perilous journey to the beaches of Normandy, Special Services units handed out comfort items, from packs of cigarettes to candy. But one item was more sought after than …

absaetze.t: On June 5, 1944, as soldiers lined British shores, preparing for their perilous journey to the beaches of Normandy, Special Services units handed out comfort items, from packs of cigarettes to candy. But one item was more sought after than any other: books. Crouched on the crowded decks awaiting Eisenhower’s call to launch, the men clasped their standard-issue rifles and clutched their standard-issue paperbacks. They were armed with stories: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, A Tree Grows in Brooklyn, The Robe, all printed to uniform-pocket size and stamped “Armed Services Edition.”

War changed this through the efforts of the newly founded Council on Books in Wartime, which redesigned and popularized the mass-produced paperback, shipping 1,324 titles and 122,951,031 copies to soldiers and sailors serving across the globe.

Armed Services Editions were revolutionary for the unique wartime need they perfectly met, and for the remarkable organizational success of the entities that together produced them. The story of these books themselves is one worth reading and reflecting on, particularly as we contemplate the needs and well-being of today’s servicemembers.

As Adolf Hitler orchestrated the burning of books across Germany, scorching their democratic past, President Franklin D. Roosevelt asserted “books cannot be killed by fire,” and his administration organized book drives alongside those for scrap metal and rubber to support the war effort. Some of these books made it to military base libraries, but you can’t arm G.I.s with oversized hardcovers. Seeing a niche need just months after the Pearl Harbor attack, the Council on Books in Wartime formed as a group to champion the concept of books as “weapons in the war of ideas.” The Council brought together key players from across the print industry: publishing house magnates from W.W. Norton and Random House, editors from the New York Times and Publishers Weekly, and leaders from the American Booksellers Association and the Book Publishers Bureau. Despite their disparate backgrounds, the nascent Council soon adopted a mission: figure out how to mass-produce and mass-supply books at production cost for the Army and Navy.

The organization had an idea, but no concept of what these books should look like, so they recruited Raymond Trautman, a young officer leading the Army’s Library Section. Trautman then recruited Stanley Thompson, a graphic artist with experience designing lightweight novels. Trautman and Thompson tackled the design and manufacturing challenges of the new paperback, overhauling rotary presses used for pulp magazines to produce their new pocket models and printing two books at a time side by side with normal presses, then cutting them in half before binding. Meanwhile, the Council debated what books should actually be printed and how they could cheaply allocate royalties. The result: the Armed Services Edition. Armed Services Editions were printed in two sizes — one as small as a postcard to fit in a uniform breast pocket, and one a bit larger to fit in the hip pocket, both oriented horizontally like flip books to conserve space. Authors whose titles were printed would receive 1 cent per copy split between them and their publisher. The first titles chosen were ones to keep young men engaged and inspired: literary classics and histories, Westerns, popular novels of the day, and a little bit of romantic smut.

The first Armed Services Edition shipment in 1943 totaled 1.5 million copies of these tiny printing novelties and was a whopping success, all to the credit of the Council on Books in Wartime and the team of passionate, relevant experts assembled to achieve their mission. Civilians from uppity and artistic fields united to support Army and Navy military communities completely foreign to them. The Council altruistically engaged in a paperback manufacturing initiative counter to their print culture yet managed a budget that still paid authors and publishers and garnered modest commercial success for their efforts. This pioneering partnership between a civilian committee and the U.S. military succeeded because all parties recognized a unique need and deployed rapidly, smartly, and selflessly to meet it.

As news of Armed Services Editions’ popularity among soldiers and sailors made its way back home, the Council began to recognize just how much these books were improving the daily lives of these men at war. But not even the Council could have predicted how the discovery of literature would impact returning veterans for decades to come.

Before the war, fourth grade was the widely accepted adequate education level for U.S. adults. Many young enlistees had never tried to read a work of literature cover to cover. During long transits across the Pacific and quiet lulls in combat zones, these servicemembers had little in the way of distraction, but they did have a book in their pocket. Eventually they opened them. Soon they would devour them, trade them like currency, and report them to be “as popular as pinup girls” — just about the highest form of praise possible from a young soldier.

Years after the war ended, one Armed Services Edition author, Helene MacInnes, received a letter from a G.I. enclosed with a copy of his Ph.D. diploma. He’d never read a book until he was given an Armed Services Edition copy of her suspense novel While Still We Live. He enjoyed the piece so much he applied for college after his service and went on to pursue a doctorate in literature. Though not every soldier pursued higher education to the doctoral level, a staggering number came home and applied for college. Servicemembers’ newfound exposure to the written word, coupled with the passage of landmark government-funded education incentives, like the G.I. Bill, encouraged nearly 7.8 million veterans to utilize education or training benefits, and of those, 2.2 million specifically to attend college. Of the 15.6 million surviving servicemembers, 50 percent used the benefit, and over 14 percent could afford college because of it. It was these educated veterans who helped form the backbone of America’s thriving middle class in the 1950s and 1960s. Veterans who would instill a love of learning in their families — multiplying numbers of books on shelves and diplomas on walls in countless homes over generations.

Of the veterans who weren’t thirsting for a diploma following the end of the war, they had at the very least developed a taste for literature, and they were used to it in paperback form. In 1939, fewer than 200,000 paperbacks were printed in the United States. By 1950, paperback publishers were popping up left and right, printing nearly 650 separate titles that year and selling over 200 million copies — more books sold than if every adult in the country bought one at the time. A cultural revolution had occurred, changing American publishing for good. Paperback book sales represented a significant percentage of the market. General book sales were at all-time highs resulting from individual purchases by a thriving, eager middle-class consumer, as well as increasing purchase contracts with federal entities, a continuation of the civil-government partnership forged by the Council.

The coalescence of the Council on Books in Wartime serves as a shining example of civilian industry leaders who united to address a military challenge the government couldn’t solve. As today’s defense innovations move further toward the overengineered and deeply technical, perhaps it is time again to step back and consider what needs of today’s servicemembers are not fully met. What simple solutions might serve them that can be achieved with help from willing civilian partners?

When we reflect on war and all its cruelties, it is easy to focus on the most gruesome narratives and forget the few uplifting ones. Lessons learned from conflict need not always be tactical or technical. Remembering the World War II love story between the G.I. and the paperback affirms this. It also reminds us that soldiers, sailors, and marines were then, and are still, warriors, but humans too. They deserve human pleasures and escapes, for who knows how far such gifts might take them.

Alana Davis is an active-duty U.S. naval submarine officer who has served in the Western Pacific and the Middle East aboard submarines and on naval staffs. She holds a BA from Harvard University and an MBA from the University of Florida. Her published writing ranges from research-based commentary to literary fiction. items.titel: MBDA’s high-speed strike missile to have range ‘far’ exceeding Exocet
items.anriss: PARIS — MBDA targets a range for its future high-speed strike missile Status RS that will be “far, far, far” more than of the Exocet anti-ship missile with its more than 200-kilometer range, said Olivier Gauffin, the company’s deputy …

absaetze.t: PARIS — MBDA targets a range for its future high-speed strike missile Status RS that will be “far, far, far” more than of the Exocet anti-ship missile with its more than 200-kilometer range, said Olivier Gauffin, the company’s deputy director for sales and business development, at a briefing at the Euronaval maritime-defense exhibition on Tuesday.

The high supersonic missile will cover four missions, including deep strike and anti-ship strike, suppression and destruction of enemy air defenses, as well as strikes against large aircraft including airborne warning systems and tankers, Gauffin said.

Stratus RS, for rapid strike, is being developed for France and the United Kingdom, and MBDA is awaiting a development contract from France’s Directorate General for Armament on behalf of the two partners. The company is simultaneously working on a stealthy subsonic cruise missile with a larger warhead called Stratus LO, for low observable, on behalf of France, the U.K. and Italy.

“The goal is very clear, it’s to face the threat of the decades to come, and we have two options to do it, which are complementary,” Gauffin said. “One is more a Ferrari, and the other is more a truck, a stealth truck.”

NATO has called on allies in Europe to rebuild offensive capabilities, as the alliance faces an aggressive Russia on its eastern flank. Stratus RS in particular would fill a gap in the inventory of European militaries, which mostly lack weapons able to destroy enemy air defenses.

The high-speed missile will be able to combine very low or very high trajectories to defeat hard-to-destroy targets such as frigates and destroyers or ground-based air defense systems, according to Gauffin. The missile will have a liquid ramjet engine that can be throttled, and will be highly maneuverable, the MBDA executive said.

Stratus RS will have a radio-frequency seeker combined with synthetic aperture radar, which provides the missile with a land-attack and a top-attack capability, according to Gauffin, who said Thales is providing the seeker technology. The idea for the slower, stealthy missile is to have only passive radio-frequency and infrared sensors, and no radar.

While the equipment in the Stratus RS missile will be new, it will be based on technology MBDA uses in other missiles, the executive said. The company has already done “a lot of trials” around the critical components, including propulsion, seeker, warhead and data management, and full development of the missile is expected to start “very soon,” Gauffin said.
MBDA uses ramjet technology in its Meteor air-to-air missile.

Both Stratus missiles will be able to be air-launched from platforms including Dassault Aviation’s Rafale jet, the Eurofighter Typhoon as well as the future aircraft being developed as part of the British-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Programme, with a size and mass “very close” to the Storm Shadow cruise missile. The missiles will use a booster for launch from ships or land.
MBDA expects flight testing of both Stratus missiles to start before the end of the decade, with the missiles to enter in service at the beginning of the 2030s.

The size of the Stratus RS means it’s not compatible with NATO-standard size torpedo tubes, meaning the missile is not envisaged as being submarine launched, according to Gauffin. For vertical launch, the missile would require a new, wider version of Naval Group’s Sylver vertical launch system, though Gauffin said there would be no change to the shipborne space occupied by the VLS.

The company also presented details on a new version of its Naval Cruise Missile, with production to start in early 2030. The updated version will be more resistant to satellite-navigation jamming, with increased survivability and new sensors, and keep the same size but with increased range and lethality, said Sophie Bourdais, vice-president for strike at MBDA.
Bourdais declined to provide specifics on the range of the Naval Cruise Missile in either its current or future iteration, other than to say it is more than 1,000 km.

The updated missile will also benefit from new mission-preparation software called Fastrike that cuts target planning down to minutes from hours, according to Bourdais. MBDA plans to integrate the capability in the Storm Shadow/Scalp EG cruise missile and the current version of the Naval Cruise Missile before 2030, the executive said.
The Naval Cruise Missile was presented as part of the European Long-range Strike Approach, and there is interest from a number of countries in the land-based variant MBDA has developed.

MBDA is still waiting for a development contract from the DGA for the updated Naval Cruise Missile. The production line for the missile in France is inactive but remains in place, and can be restarted to produce the updated version, according to Bourdais.

items.titel: Please Don’t Put in the Novel That I Died: Olivia Manning’s (Lightly) Fictionalized Novels
items.anriss: “I don’t want fame when I am dead,” Olivia Manning once complained. “I want it now.” Manning, the British novelist who died in 1980, carried grudges: never made the Booker shortlist, never got a “solo review” in the Sunday papers, always …

absaetze.t: “I don’t want fame when I am dead,” Olivia Manning once complained. “I want it now.” Manning, the British novelist who died in 1980, carried grudges: never made the Booker shortlist, never got a “solo review” in the Sunday papers, always passed over for Iris Murdoch. Manning’s best-known work, her “Balkan” trilogy inspired by her experience in Romania and Greece during World War II, was reissued by the NYRB in 2010 with a praiseful introduction by Rachel Cusk, but Manning would have wondered what took so long.
Article continues after advertisement

“Manning’s ‘people’ are more than literary characters: they have the feeling of real beings who happen to find themselves in the narrative frame, like passersby caught on camera,” wrote Cusk. “Indeed, The Balkan Trilogy is frequently so faithful to the sense of lived life that it is often difficult to discern the hand that is shaping it.” You can understand the appeal of Manning’s fiction to Cusk in particular. About the same time that Cusk wrote this introduction, she was sued by some of her “people,” a family who recognized themselves in her memoir The Last Supper.

Not noted in Cusk’s introduction to Manning’s Balkan Trilogy is that Manning also got in libel trouble over those same novels. One of the terrible things about such an action is how it can compromise the work. “The American edition got lawyered to death,” said Cusk of The Last Supper. “It’s a slightly butchered corpse, that one.”

What may be worse than having one’s book butchered by lawyers is having the butchering done incorrectly, as happened to Manning. The inconsistent censorship of Manning’s Balkan trilogy introduced an error into one of the novels that, for 60 years, appears to have gone unnoticed. If it had been noticed, Manning would have complained about it.
Manning’s three Balkan novels are her most acclaimed, though one contemporary reader told her that in a semi-autobiographical novel “it is just so easy to put down what happened.”

But Manning always pulled from life. A prim, petty matron in her 1951 School for Love was inspired by Robert Graves’s sister Clarissa, but where Clarissa was tall, Manning made her character short. Clarissa nonetheless noticed and considered a lawsuit. Manning’s friend, the poet Steve Smith, wrote a “bitchy review” of Manning’s The Doves of Venus, after finding a character much like herself in its pages: neurotic, and terrified of the dentist. This despite Manning changing Smith’s height.

Manning’s husband, Reggie Smith (no relation to Stevie), once cautioned: “You may be able to pull the wool over the eyes of the Sunday Times readers, but there will always be those who know the truth.”

In 1967, Manning finally heard from somebody’s lawyers. “An awful thing has happened to me,” she wrote to her friend. In the first two books of her Balkan Trilogy, The Great Fortune (1960) and The Spoilt City (1962), Manning had referred to the 1939 assassination of Armand Cǎlinescu, the Romanian prime minister, by Romania’s fascist Iron Guard. Manning and her husband were in Romania when it had happened. Drawing as she often did from real life, Manning described Cǎlinescu’s death, and how, a year later, each member of his surviving family were “taken to the nearest large town and shot in the marketplace.” The original assassination was implied to have been done for the benefit, or with the participation, of Romania’s King Carol: “You never heard that the King said… ‘I’ll get that bastard Cǎlinescu if it’s the last thing I ever do’?”

But in fact Cǎlinescu’s family had not been shot in the streets, and his son, Barbu Cǎlinecsu was living and working in Cambridge, as an architect. The younger Cǎlinecsu was “libelled and deeply damaged by things said about his family and father” in Manning’s novel. For one thing, the claim that King Carol supported his father’s assassination was baseless. But his biggest concern, as it was told to Manning’s publishers, Heinemann and Panther, that if its description of events were to be taken by a reader on good faith, they would conclude that Barbu Cǎlinescu was murdered in Romania after his father, and therefore that the Cambridge architect with the same name was “a liar and imposter.” Barbu Cǎlinescu sought not just damages but to have the two novels withdrawn from print and for Manning and her publishers to publicly apologize.
“I feel pretty sick when I think of it,” Manning wrote to a friend.

Manning’s error was in fact an error, not a deliberate fiction. But the threat still worried her, and her publishers. “The law of libel is so confusing that everyone says something different,” she wrote. “Even the solicitors seem vague about it. That is the worst of it—a British jury is liable to do anything.”
“What a good thing you are insured against libel,” Manning said to the managing director at Heinemann’s.
“Yes,” he replied, “but you are not.”

The kind of claim brought by Barbu Cǎlinescu was not uncommon—but in centuries past, when the form of the novel was not so well-defined in the culture. A literary critic might have been able to marshal a sophisticated defence against Cǎlinescu’s argument. Why should a reader assume that what they read in a novel, as opposed to a memoir or a work of history, was true, or take the novelist’s word for it over the evidence of their eyes and ears? Yes, Manning’s novel was semi-autobiographical, but it had given fictional names to the characters based on real people, which included her and her husband. Might that not signify to a reader that the whole novel was, in a sense, untrue? Catherine Gallagher, in her 2006 essay “The Rise of Fictionality,” identified a reader’s ability to apprehend a realistic, plausible story—like those written by Manning—as fiction to be a sign of “fictional sophistication in a culture.”
If she ever paid attention to how her books had been censored she never said much about it. The real effect of the episode was to put her on high alert of being sued again.

But few readers of fiction have had the experience of a novel identifying them, personally, as having been dead for 20 years, and so perhaps we cannot understand the impacts. Even Manning, in her private correspondence, referred to Barbu Cǎlinescu as the man “claiming to be the son of the assassinated prime minister.” Her instinct was to trust her own novel.

Manning’s publishers settled the case. Cǎlinescu accepted an apology, amendments to the books, and reimbursement for his costs. As to those, Manning fought her publisher Heinemann. “The firm did not commit the libel,” Heinemann told her. Manning argued that if one was going to publish a writer who draws their material from life, things like this were bound to happen. She threatened to leave the publisher if they forced her to pay, and the matter was “quietly forgotten.”

The Spoilt City was recalled and amended, with all references to an execution of Armand Cǎlinescu’s family expunged. Panther, who published Manning in paperback, initially mishandled the amendments, leaving a plural reference to “the slaughtered Cǎlinescus” intact. It was corrected in a later edition.

Gone too were the suggestions that King Carol had wanted his prime minister dead, which was principally expressed in a line of dialogue in The Great Fortune. The character Galpin says to the character Yakimov, “You never heard that the King said to Udureanu: ‘I’ll get that bastard Cǎlinescu if it’s the last thing I ever do’?” This was removed.

But a reference later in the book to that line of dialogue was not. In another conversation between Galpin and Yakimov about King Carol, Yakimov asks says, “You said he said he’d get Cǎlinescu.” But Galpin hadn’t said, not in any edition of the book published since 1967. A reader might conclude that the line refers to a conversation these characters have had off the page. Instead, it’s a clue, the only indication that the book is not the original text.

What’s confusing about the retention of this line is that it seems to imply Carol’s complicity in the assassination just as much as the expurgated dialogue did. It has remained in the book to this day, untouched and—probably by the Cǎlinescu family, at least—unnoticed.

Manning wrote all of this off as “a sad business.” If she ever paid attention to how her books had been censored she never said much about it. The real effect of the episode was to put her on high alert of being sued again.

The character of Yakimov, a comic, amoral scrounger whom Rachel Cusk described as Manning’s “masterpiece,” was like many of Manning’s characters inspired by a real person. So pathetic was the portrait, though, that Manning made especial effort to disguise her inspiration. After the Cǎlinescu case, a woman approached Manning at a party to say that she was “greatly amused” by her books because she were acquainted with the source material for Yakimov. Manning said she was mistaken. Then the woman named the person: the British writer Derek Patmore.

“I begged her on no account ever to mention the books to him and she promised, very sweetly, to keep the whole thing dark but the incident made me feel so ill I had to leave the party,” Manning described it.

Patmore, like everyone else in this story, is long dead. If Patmore were alive, he’d have bigger problems than Manning: One of the five sentences in Patmore’s Wikipedia biography is a piece of thirdhand gossip alleging that he was a pederast.

If Manning learned anything from the Cǎlinescu case, it was to make sure that the people she was writing about were really dead. In Cairo, during the Second World War, Manning had witnessed an eight-year-old boy killed by a mortar shell, and the boy’s parents, in denial, attempting to revive the child by feeding him gruel through the hole in his cheek. Three decades later, Manning put it in a book. The author Penelope Lively called this “one of the most insensitive translations of experience into fiction.”

By publication, both the child’s parents were deceased. The family’s solicitors nonetheless wrote to Manning, demanding that the scene and the characters in it be removed from the novel and all future works. This time Manning stood her ground. Manning wrote back defending her creation, Angela Hooper, as bearing no resemblance at all to Amy Smart, the mother of that eight-year-old child. Manning explicated the differences: nationality, race, temperament. The most obvious difference, which Manning left unsaid, was that in the novel Angela Hooper goes on to be great friends with the character based on Olivia Manning. In life, Amy Smart invited Olivia Manning to one dinner party; she was then barred from the house due to what one biographer has called a “carping and vindictive personality.”
A mutual acquaintance of both women once said to Manning, “I should think you must be one of the happiest of women.”
“Why?”
“Because you do most successfully that which you set out to do.”
“And what is that?”
“Be as unpleasant as possible to as many people as possible.”

Manning, I think, would have thought that that is part of being a novelist. And she would not necessarily be wrong, nor alone. “At this point, I feel it’s a form of social embarrassment how everything I do turns up in my next book,” said Rachel Cusk in 2010. “I used to worry about that sort of thing all the time, and now I don’t. I’m completely shameless.”

This article refers to the two published biographies of Olivia Manning, Olivia Manning: A Life, by Neville Braybrooke and June Braybrooke (Chatto & Windus 2004), and Olivia Manning: A Woman at War, by Deirdre David (Oxford University Press 2012), and previously unpublished material from Manning’s papers, held at the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin.

items.titel: Building a Community of Imposters: What It Means To Be a Literary Translator Today
items.anriss: Gracias for your recent note. It came, as you say, “out of the blue,” an expression that, in and of itself, defies translation. In my native Spanish, one would say “ de la nada ,” not out of nowhere, since that would be “ de ningún lugar …

absaetze.t: Gracias for your recent note. It came, as you say, “out of the blue,” an expression that, in and of itself, defies translation. In my native Spanish, one would say “de la nada,” not out of nowhere, since that would be “de ningún lugar,” but out of nothingness. Nothingness is a word that frightens me. It is similar to nothing, but with an added philosophical twist. Whenever I stumble upon it, I think of Fernando Pessoa: “Não sou nada. Nunca serei nada. Não posso querer ser nada. À parte isso, tenho em mim todos os sonhos do mundo.” Rendered into a rough English from Portuguese: “I am nothing. I will never be anything. I couldn’t want to be nothing. Besides that, I have in me all the dreams of the world.” But maybe the first line should be amended to “I am nothingness,” since Pessoa is talking about the condition of unimportance.

But excuse the detour: your letter is anything but unimportant. Among many other things, you ask me about “impersonating” famous poets, referring to the poems I shared in class purportedly written by Akhmatova, Celan, Drummond de Andrade, and Hikmet. You say you’re still thinking of them, in spite of all the time that has gone by.
You ask why I compose poetry from someone else’s perspective. Is it not fraudulent? What if any of these “originals” is confused by readers with a true work by these authors? Are you “passing”?

My answer might not satisfy you. Or else, it might disgust you. Chanelling someone else’s voice is what translators do. Why not go a step further, expanding the oeuvre of established poets? In some cases (Petrarch, Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Cervantes, Shakespaere, Borges, Amichai), I have spent years studying their mannerisms. Maybe I’m a vampire, sucking blood to remain remain alive.

And do I know all the languages I write in? Not all. I take after writers who have engaged in a similar feat: Samuel Beckett translated Mexican poetry with astonishing success. He had learned Spanish and French as a student at Trinity College, Dublin. But while French was essential to him (En attendant Godot began in French and then was self-translated into English), for some reason he avoided Spanish in his life. Still, his renditions in An Anthology of Mexican Poetry, compiled by Octavio Paz, completed in 1950 but not published until 1958, are astonishing. The project, sponsored by UNESCO, was part of a larger international cultural effort, though it was a task that Beckett reportedly found challenging.

Likewise, Richard Wilbur, known for his renditions of Molière and Racine, also translated from Russian (Akmatova and Brodsky), Spanish (Borges, Guillén), Italian (Dante, Quasimodo), as well as Portuguese, Bulgarian, Romanian, and Latin. Ursula K. LeGuin’s translation of the Tao Te Ching by Lao Tzu, done even though LeGuin didn’t know Chinese. And W. S. Merwin translated from Dahomey and Quechua. These are just a few examples.

Like myself, the translators depend on an “insider” or on another language to reach the original. But you’re right: I have gone further: before or after doing my translations, I have created new originals. I have done this with the help of friends, colleagues, and, in some heteronymous cases, through A.I.
Once I started writing, I realized I could be an impostor as well. There is no shame in literary impostorship, only freedom.
Am I masquerading? Am I a charlatan? Yes, you are right: my biggest influence—the father figure I emutale—is Cervantes.
The real questions behind this endeavor are relatively simple: Are these good poems? And do they offer a fresh lens through which to appreciate the original author?

You say you remember the poems I brought after Mallarmé, Apollinaire, and Paul Valèry. That makes me happy. I like the the rhyming patterns of my Mallarmé and Valéry. (By the way, have you read Valéry’s “Le Cimetière marin,” set in the cemetery at Sète (where Valéry himself is now buried)? That haunting last stanza is memorable:

Le vent se lève!…il faut tenter de vivre! L’air immense ouvre et referme mon livre, La vague en poudre ose jaillir des rocs! Envolez-vous, pages tout éblouies! Rompez, vagues! Rompez d’eaux réjouies Ce toit tranquille où picoraient des focs!

I’m not sure about the counting of the syllables for the classical alexandrine verse (12 “feet”) and “uneven” verse (vers impair, defined by Verlaine in “L’art poétique”). In my Mallarmé, some lines may be too short (11 feet) or too long (13 feet), because of the “e muet” rule in classical French verse.
Anyway, here is another “fake original.” If you didn’t keep a copy of my previous version, lemme know. I can send you a PDF:
“Sur la Tombe” de Stéphane Mallarmé
Sous ce marbre muet, où les songes sommeillent, Le dernier souffle d’encre au soir s’émerveille. Mille vers se tressant s’élancent, disparus, Ne roulant plus leur or dans l’ombre des perdus.
Échos des mots—éclats de voix éteintes, Labyrinthe du cœur, ses flammes étreintes. Ici, dans la poussière, un reste se dépose, Tandis que le Temps meurt, et lentement explose.
Sous cette pierre dort le songe tissé d’ombre, Fin de la syllabe et de la pensée sombre. Un frémissement plane au bord de son essor, Un soupir s’éteint dans l’infini sans corps.
Quel monde reste-t-il quand tout se tait encore? La plume est un océan où l’âme s’évapore. Dans le vers vide on cherche un infini brisé, Dernier souffle: cercueil, silence, vérité.
Ô lettres frémissantes en la main de la mort, Vous partez—mais gardez le secret du sort. La tombe est un miroir sans rumeur, sans mémoire, Rendant l’écho muet du néant, du miroir.
Ainsi, dans la poussière, un feu pur se soulève, Dans l’étreinte de mort, le dernier mot s’achève.

All to say that I remember you fondly from your student days. In the classroom, you were bright and inquisitive, always adding insightful comments to our collective discussion. And your passion for language was infectious. You frequently landed on words, using them not only to say what you wanted but as snippets of information onto themselves. I particularly recall a moment when, amidst a discussion on the difference between the house and home, you said the first was physical and the second imaginary. Imaginary—you made clear to the rest of us that home is an artifice, an illusion, “por arte de magia”—an act of magic.
You might be surprised the quote still echoes in my mind. I think about it often: home as an act of magic. You were right.

It has taken me longer than expected to respond to you because first, it goes without saying that your request—to explain why I became a translator in the first place, my misgivings along the way, and “to grant advice about how to translate in an age of perplexity” where “everything seems to come to us at frantic speed”—needs careful calibration. I have spent long hours thinking how to go about responding to the letter. Honestly, my first reaction was to ignore it: out of sight, out of mind. Why, in this most agitated sea of responsibilities, should one interrupt the flux of things, to explain how an inadvertent aspect in one’s upbringing, in time but without clear explanation, became a central life theme?

Yet if we don’t do that—stop the world in order to reflect on what matters—death will visit us, unannounced, as it is wont to do, and then, kaboom, as we look into infinity, we will realize we gave up the opportunity of streamlining one’s thoughts, of making a coherent narrative of ourselves following a particular thread, of explaining why we are who we are.

You ask if translation is a worthy life pursuit, since your love for it is immense but “remuneration is meager.” I’m not sure that continues to be the case. Yes, although translators still aren’t fully recognized as embarking on “intellectual work” (as you know, it remains unacknowledged in tenure case), the landscape is changing rapidly. More and more schools have opened translation programs. In labor disputes, there are associations that defend the rights of translators. There are prizes specifically for translators, such as the National Book Award, ALTA, and others, and the Booker Prize for International Fiction now gives an award to the best novel in translation that is divided equally between author and translator. Along the way, the media pays more attention to translation issues.

At Restless Books, which as you know is devoted to contemporary world literature in translation, the translator’s name always appears—prominently—on the cover. After acquiring a book, matching the sensibility of the author with that of the translator is, in my view, the most important decision an editor makes. We are in no way outliers, although, it is true, corporate publishers still lag behind, considering the translator’s job as second or third tier.

The other way, I was rereading Ovid’s Metamorphosis. I had been translating into English Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz’s powerful self-defense Response to Sor Filotea, written at the request of her confessor. In it, she talks about the Greek mythical figure of Phaethon, the son of Helius, who asks his father to allow him to drive a chariot to the sun. Ovid narrates Phaethon’s ordeal in the last section of Book One and the first of Book Two. In her daring to challenge the hierarchical structure of the Catholic Church in colonial Mexico, Sor Juana identified with Phaethon’s daring, know that she herself might likely die in her journey to intellectual enlightenment.

Then, by happenstance, I also opened a volume of Shakespeare’s poems and delved into Venus and Adonis, which he published in 1593, before he produced any of his masterpieces. The volume is also based on a section of Metamorphosis, where the unifying theme is change: constant, endless, unexpected change.

Sor Juana read Ovid in Latin, whereas Shakespeare knew, read, and borrowed from Arthur Golding’s translation of 1567, just as he borrowed from John Florio’s English translation of Montaigne’s essays, from which he also lifted a few passages, including parts of “Of the Cannibals,” in his play The Tempest.
Translators aren’t parrots, repeating a line in a new tongue. They are archeologists of our verbal reservoir, recognizing what words belong to which epoch.

Translation is a pivot for writers from around the world to find each other. Shakespeare’s education remains a mystery. How could a young man from Stratford-upon-Avon, who didn’t finish his schooling, have such learning on the classics, geography, philology, politics, and the human heart? The answer—not often said aloud these days of pluralistic fervor—is that school isn’t for everyone. Some are “autodidactas”—Spanish for self-taught. The best school isn’t necessarily the classroom. But whatever space it might take place in, it always, without except, requires the discovery, even in our age of computers, iPhones, tablets, and other technological devices, of the written page.

And that written page is often about foreignness—e.g., translation. In her private apartment in the convent of San Jerónimo, Sor Juana too had a personal library of about 4,000 volumes. They were in Greek, Latin, Spanish, Portuguese, and perhaps Hebrew. As she describes in Response to Sor Filotea, her learning was done solo, seldom with the help of a teacher but on her own.

I’m fond of Sor Juana’s interest in a type of Nahuatl poetry known as tocotines. Nahuatl was the language of the Aztec empire when the Spanish conquistadors arrived to what is Mexico today in the 16th century. Nahuatl quickly became a repressed—forbidden—language. Sor Juana owned a slave girl and had an indigenous young woman as a helper in her apartment. That maid likely spoke Nahuatl.

items.titel: Du Palais de Tokyo au ministère de la Culture, pourquoi le monde de l’art se passionne pour la ruralité
items.anriss: En 2024, le ministère de la Culture lançait le “Printemps de la ruralité”, avant de …

absaetze.t: Le phénomène n’est pas nouveau, loin de là. N’est-ce pas à Barbizon, en pleine forêt de Fontainebleau, que l’on marche dans les pas de peintres qui ont révolutionné la peinture de paysage ? À Giverny, petit village de l’Eure, que les touristes du monde entier accourent pour visiter la maison de Monet ?

Depuis longtemps fréquentée et habitée par des artistes en quête de calme et de beauté, la campagne a pourtant bel et bien changé de statut. Jusqu’au début du XIXe siècle, elle ne faisait qu’offrir aux peintres pléthore d’adorables visions pastorales, dans lesquelles ils allaient jusqu’à glisser de charmantes figures pour l’idéaliser – on pourra penser aux œuvres de Nicolas Poussin, John Constable. Puis, des artistes comme Jean-François Millet, Rosa Bonheur ou, plus récemment, la photographe Madeleine de Sinéty, ont eu à cœur de représenter la réalité des paysans ainsi que leur labeur.

Aujourd’hui, la campagne incarne pour les artistes et qui s’y intéressent un territoire complexe traversé de tensions politiques, sociales et économiques, comme en témoigne avec éloquence le travail de Suzanne Husky (née en 1975) : en 2016, celle-ci a cocréé avec Stéphanie Sagot le « Nouveau Ministère de l’Agriculture » pour développer toutes sortes de projets, et fait de chacune de ses œuvres un manifeste pour la protection de l’environnement, comme lorsqu’elle détourne la tapisserie de La Dame à la licorne : « Là où il y avait des licornes et des sirènes, j’ai placé un bulldozer ».
La campagne, un vivier d’initiatives militantes

Dans la même veine, les expositions de la curatrice Julie Crenn sonnent l’alarme depuis plusieurs années, en 2021 au Transpalette de Bourges ou en 2024 aux Abattoirs de Toulouse. Fondatrice du programme de résidences « Agir dans son lieu », elle propose à des artistes de travailler en milieu rural et de cocréer avec des paysans, dont ils ne sont pas si différents : « Artistes et paysans sont complètement écrasés par leurs systèmes », nous expliquait-elle ainsi il y a deux ans.

Et si, depuis les années 1980, les centres d’art et les résidences d’artistes se sont multipliés dans les territoires ruraux (citons le Centre international d’art et du paysage de l’île de Vassivière en Haute-Vienne, le « lieu de création et de répit » La Broussaille dans la Creuse ou encore Rurart, le seul centre d’art contemporain placé sous la tutelle du ministère de l’Agriculture), ceux-ci regorgent de plus en plus d’initiatives collectives, militantes, engagées, pleinement investies par les (jeunes) artistes.

En 2017, Olga Boudin (née en 1991) a ainsi quitté avec une poignée d’amis les Beaux-Arts de Paris où elle étudiait jusqu’alors pour installer un atelier collectif dans un bâtiment de la petite commune de Lacelle, en Corrèze. « C’était juste après les manifestations contre la loi Travail », se souvient-elle aujourd’hui. « On s’était rapproché sur des questions davantage politiques qu’esthétiques. » Le petit groupe choisit alors la Corrèze par conviction, inspiré par l’identité du plateau de Millevaches, « où s’inscrit toute une histoire d’expérimentations sociales un peu alternatives ». Rapidement, les artistes s’investissent dans la vie du village. Ils organisent des expositions, des concerts, réussissent grâce à une aide du centre d’art de Vassivière à « réaliser une œuvre collective, rouvrir des chemins communaux : ça a permis de faire comprendre à des gens du village qu’on était là pour s’investir ».
Être artiste loin des villes

Bien sûr, quelques-uns ne s’y feront jamais, les considérant comme des néo-ruraux qui ne peuvent tout à fait s’intégrer. « Ce sont des questions identitaires auxquelles on n’a pas envie de répondre. » Mais l’investissement des artistes est sincère, au point qu’Olga Boudin s’est engagée au sein du conseil municipal dès 2020, et a même été élue maire de Lacelle il y a quelques mois (devenant au passage la première maire transgenre de France). Pas de quoi la faire toutefois renoncer à ses activités de peinture, d’édition et de graphisme. « Je connais beaucoup de maires qui sont agriculteurs par ailleurs. Quand on est artiste, on a un peu les mêmes problématiques, le travail ne s’arrête jamais vraiment. Ça peut fonctionner ensemble, mais ça reste à inventer », confie-t-elle, car elle doit désormais réfléchir à deux fois avant d’oser postuler pour une résidence ou tout autre projet un peu engageant, sachant que la mairie l’occupe jusqu’à plusieurs jours par semaine.

Du petit groupe avec lequel elle est arrivée à Lacelle, deux sont repartis sur l’argument « de ne pas gagner assez leur vie et de ne pas faire pas assez de rencontres ». Mais pour sa part, elle relativise : « J’ai l’impression qu’en ville, il y a une telle concurrence que ça ne changerait rien ! ». Elle se réjouit aussi d’avoir trouvé « un rythme à soi beaucoup plus lent et personnel qu’en ville », et « d’avoir un récit un peu singulier ». D’autant que les institutions sont de plus en plus nombreuses à s’y intéresser.
De Toulouse à New York, de nombreuses expositions sur le sujet

Outre la grande exposition de 70 chefs-d’œuvre du Centre Pompidou « À travers champs » au musée Crozatier du Puy-en-Velay en 2024, autour des artistes du XXe siècle qui ont pris la campagne pour sujet, il y a eu la grande exposition « Artistes et paysans » au musée des Abattoirs de Toulouse, déjà citée, et on attend « PaySans » au Mucem à partir de février 2027. Dans le monde, la même tendance s’observe : à New York, l’architecte superstar Rem Koolhaas a présenté en 2020 au Guggenheim « Countryside, The Future », une vaste exposition qui explorait « les transformations radicales affectant les territoires ruraux, isolés et sauvages », tandis que le collectif Inland, dirigé par l’artiste Fernando García-Dory et basé en Espagne, travaille depuis 2009 à proposer des stratégies de revitalisation des campagnes et d’action écologique, en organisant aussi bien des formations pour bergers que des commandes de projets artistiques.

Ces jours-ci, la curatrice Liza Maignan présente « Toi et ta bande » au Palais de Tokyo, une passionnante exposition collective – à laquelle participe Olga Boudin – qui aborde « l’écologie des relations qui se créent sur ces territoires-là », nous détaille la commissaire, convoquant aussi bien des pratiques artistiques que des modes de vie et de travail alternatifs et des actions militantes. Elle-même a étudié aux Beaux-Arts de Toulouse et a participé à la création du collectif Silo à Cannes-et-Clairan, dans le Gard. Les recherches permises par une bourse d’écriture de la fondation Pernod Ricard (qui a donné lieu à la publication de son texte « Rumeurs des villes ») lui ont permis de creuser le sujet et d’approcher de près les réseaux de jeunes artistes qui fertilisent ces territoires de la création à la campagne, en haute montagne et dans les îles.
« D’autres modèles économiques, un mode de vie moins violent »

Selon elle, la tendance s’inscrit dans « une suite logique de mouvements qui existent depuis longtemps, même avant les années 1970 », et dépasse la simple question économique : il ne s’agit plus seulement de dénicher un grand atelier pour moins cher, mais de « trouver d’autres modèles économiques, d’être dans un mode de vie moins violent ». Elle souligne aussi que les artistes et collectifs choisis, comme Elsa Brès, Fossile Futur ou Brieuc Schieb, se sont installés dans des lieux comme « la Bretagne, les Cévennes, la Corrèze, où il y a d’importants historiques de luttes » et où les associations comme les initiatives d’autogestion ou les lieux communautaires sont nombreux.

Certains se nourrissent directement de ce contexte de production particulier, comme les artistes du collectif Le Transfo, dont l’implantation dans les Hautes-Pyrénées est fondatrice : « Le contexte local, marqué par un fort engagement en faveur de la préservation de l’environnement, du pastoralisme et d’un tourisme durable, nourrit directement les projets artistiques », revendiquent-ils ainsi sur leur site. Mais au contraire des artistes du land art qui prenaient la terre pour matière première, Liza Maignan a aussi voulu insister sur une indépendance des pratiques artistiques : « Il me semblait important de rappeler que les artistes qui vivent en ruralité ne parlent pas que de ruralité. Leur art peut exister au-delà du territoire où ils et elles vivent. »
Un riche tissu d’établissements culturels sur le territoire

Du côté des publics, le ministère de la Culture s’est intéressé de près à la question en 2024, avec la consultation dite « Printemps de la ruralité ». L’enquête associée laissait deviner une situation en demi-teinte : 35 % des personnes interrogées avaient visité une exposition ou un musée dans l’année, 63 % étaient allées au cinéma, 46 % déclaraient avoir eu accès à une offre culturelle itinérante (exposition, cirque, bibliobus…), 78 % estimaient habiter à moins de quinze kilomètres d’une bibliothèque ou d’une médiathèque. Mais elles étaient aussi 42 % à juger le prix des billets trop élevé, 35 % à penser que les lieux culturels étaient trop éloignés de chez eux et 38 % à juger que « l’offre proposée ne les intéresse pas »…

Parmi les solutions proposées, la ministre Rachida Dati avait notamment annoncé le lancement d’un « plan visant à développer et renforcer le réseau des artothèques sur le territoire », doté d’un budget de quatre millions d’euros. Il s’agissait ainsi de remettre en avant le système de ces bibliothèques d’œuvres d’art dispersées dans toute la France. Mais aussi de soutenir de nouveaux projets par le biais d’un appel à manifestation d’intérêt et d’encourager la mobilité des œuvres d’art en France.

Un guide des musées ruraux est également paru peu après, valorisant le déjà-là d’une France dont on ne peut nier qu’elle est déjà extrêmement riche en établissements culturels, dans tous ses départements – et les ouvertures se poursuivent. Encore tout récemment, l’ancienne cave coopérative d’Aigne, petite commune de 300 habitants dans le Minervois, est devenue La Còla, vaste lieu d’exposition et de résidences porté par l’association L’ahah.

La situation de la campagne comme « désert culturel » évolue donc de jour en jour. Surtout, on l’aura compris, grâce au dynamisme des jeunes artistes et des associations, qui rêvent d’un monde meilleur en retapant de vieilles bâtisses et en enrichissant les agendas culturels locaux, à l’écart de villes de plus en plus chères et bourgeoises.

items.titel: Alter design exhibition returns to Tokyo with AI-powered tea ceremony and washi paper furniture
items.anriss: The second edition of young designers' exhibition Alter has opened in central Tokyo , featuring a glowing lung-like lamp and Japanese cedar stools made from every part of the log.

absaetze.t: The second edition of young designers’ exhibition Alter has opened in central Tokyo, featuring a glowing lung-like lamp and Japanese cedar stools made from every part of the log.
Alter is being held at Nihonbashi Mitsu Hall during the 10th iteration of Designart Tokyo, which is ongoing across the Japanese capital.

The show brings together work from 75 international creators, mostly in their 20s or 30s, united by a desire to “re-examine the value of product design” in an industry that the exhibitors say is growing increasingly rigid in its output.
Among the offerings on display is a group show of texture-heavy design pieces curated by Dutch designer Tim Teven.

Under the title At First Contact, it includes a bright green vessel by French designer Audrey Large. Complete with protruding, tentacle-like embellishments, the vase is typical of Large’s otherworldly style.

Nearby, Dutch creative Teun Zwets presents a wall-mounted, mirrored cabinet made of his recognisably glossy lacquered split wood, while Paris studio LS Gomma contributed a polyurethane rubber scone lamp with a glowing ribbed body that loosely resembles a pair of lungs.

“The pieces’ attention to surface resonates with traditions within Japanese craft, where the effects of making, material behaviour and use remain visible in the finished object,” said Teven, who selected pieces that draw attention to “reflection, gloss and wear”.
Elsewhere, Alter presents a “tea ceremony with no host” by Tariki Research Institute, created to invert traditional Japanese tea ceremonies.

Instead of a tea master choosing the right cup for the occasion, environmental data picked up by sensors at various locations around the world is translated into organic shapes by an AI algorithm and blow-moulded into unique vessels, from which visitors were encouraged to drink.
Bole is a project by London architecture studio Pan Projects, completed in collaboration with local forestry company Morisho and Nara-based wood specialist Morisuke Mei Tree Industry.

Working with the knowledge that a typical Japanese cedar tree yields five logs, each four metres long, the collaborators made eight stools from each of these logs, cut into simple discs to use every part of the log.
For Alter, the stools are presented as a large totemic column to highlight the process.
“Today in the mountains of Japan, the market value of logs is below the value of the labour of the people who grow and care for them,” explained the show organisers.
“Even though wood continues to flow through construction and manufacturing sites, most of its value never goes back to the forest. Bole was born as a response to this imbalance.”

Also on display is Capillary Drift, a project by Japanese designer Yuma Kano, washi paper specialist Gen Taniguchi of Nao Tesuki Washi, and artisan Kurara Omichi, who works at Uchida Dyeing Factory in Tokyo.
The trio is presenting a selection of stools, vessels and other material experiments made out of delicately dyed washi paper.
“Rather than seeing washi simply as a flat surface, we approach it as a complex network of interwoven fibres, seeking to reveal expressions hidden within the material itself,” said Taniguchi.

The inaugural Alter exhibition was shown during last year’s Designart Tokyo. At the time, the exhibition team spoke to Dezeen about their desire to revive the city’s “increasingly homogenous” design scene.

Designart Tokyo 2026 takes place from 30 October to 8 November 2026 at various locations across Tokyo, Japan. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.
